strengths: Novel probabilistic decomposition: Proposition 3.3 elegantly factors trajectory-level safety into per-timestep multiplicative scores via a clever telescoping proof, enabling credit assignment from sparse labels
Well-motivated problem: Learning both unknown costs and budgets from binary trajectory labels is practical and extends prior work (RLSF) that assumes known budget
Comprehensive experiments: 12 diverse tasks across three environments with reasonable baselines (oracle, RLSF, C&B), demonstrating safe policies across all domains

Strong credit assignment analysis: Figures 3-4 convincingly show the model correctly identifies critical timesteps, allocating higher costs to steps exceeding the budget threshold and lower costs in flat regions
Clear technical presentation: Logical progression from problem setup through method to experiments with detailed appendix including training curves and ablations
weaknesses: Fundamental mismatch between problem and experiments: The paper claims the true labeling function Ψ(τ) is unknown, yet experiments label trajectories with 'a script implementing the true labeling function.' This contradicts the core problem assumption and unclear how practitioners would obtain labels

Weak empirical improvement over simpler baseline: RLSF (which only learns cost, not budget) achieves better cost than SSV on multiple tasks (PointCircle1: 1.6 vs 16.2, Walker2d: 0.3 vs 24.1, Ant: 5.8 vs 19.5), undermining the claim that learning the budget is important

Missing approximation analysis: Lemma 3.4 provides no convergence rates or error bounds; the Jensen's inequality approximation (Eq. 9) can be loose; no analysis of how well E[∑γ^t log P̂∆t] ≥ log d approximates the original constraint E[Ψ(τ)] ≥ d

Significant pre-training requirement underemphasized: Models require offline pre-training to 95% accuracy using an offline safe RL dataset with supposedly 'unknown' labels, which is itself a strong practical requirement not adequately discussed

Restrictive Assumption 3.6 under-discussed: The requirement that trajectory safety probability can only decrease limits expressiveness, yet this fundamental limitation receives minimal attention and no sensitivity analysis

Unclear trajectory selection contribution: Coefficient of variation-based selective feedback (Section C.2) lacks theoretical justification, and Table 3 shows using all trajectories often performs as well or better, undermining this proposed contribution
Missing technical details: Network architecture for fw(s,a,h) unspecified; summary vector dimensionality unclear; hyperparameters for negative lognormal decoder not provided
Limited sensitivity analysis: Only one budget value (25) tested across all experiments; no analysis of robustness to different budgets or noisy labels

strengths: Addresses a practical problem in safe RL with unknown constraints
Novel credit assignment decomposition via multiplicative per-timestep safety factors (Proposition 3.3) is mathematically elegant
Comprehensive experiments across 12 diverse continuous control tasks with multiple seeds
Generally well-written with clear architecture diagrams and problem formulation
Honest discussion of limitations and assumptions
weaknesses: Empirical results fail to demonstrate superiority over RLSF baseline—RLSF often achieves significantly lower costs (e.g., 80× better on Walker2d, 10× better on PointCircle1), undermining the paper's core contribution
Multiple compounding approximations (Lemma 3.4, Jensen's inequality, log reformulation) lack cumulative error analysis or empirical validation of their tightness
Assumption 3.6 (monotonic safety probabilities) is restrictive and insufficiently justified; many real domains violate this (e.g., energy recovery, resource accumulation)

Credit assignment validation is only qualitative (Figures 3-4); lacks quantitative metrics (correlation, MSE) between inferred and true costs; acknowledged 'delayed' credit assignment impact is unanalyzed
Problem setting motivation is weak—if binary trajectory labels are available, why is the budget unknown? The gap between oracle and zero knowledge is artificial
Selective feedback strategy shows minimal improvement over using all trajectories (Table 3), questioning whether the proposed mechanism works
Missing key reproducibility details: network architectures, hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, CV threshold selection for trajectory filtering
No code availability mentioned despite reproducibility requirements
Dense presentation covering multiple components (two models, credit assignment, reformulation, selective feedback) obscures key insights about which components matter

strengths: Addresses a practical and well-motivated problem: learning safety constraints from sparse trajectory-level labels is significantly more realistic than prior work requiring state-level feedback or known cost functions

Novel credit assignment mechanism via Proposition 3.3: elegantly decomposes trajectory safety probability into per-timestep multiplicative scores, enabling effective learning from only binary trajectory labels
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 12 diverse continuous control tasks (MuJoCo, Safety Gymnasium, Bullet) demonstrating broad applicability
Strong empirical results: SSV model achieves safety across all 12 tasks with reward close to oracle PPO-Lagrangian, often requiring fewer labeled trajectories than RLSF

Thorough credit assignment validation: Figures 3-4 convincingly show the model correctly identifies critical timesteps, with peaks around true budget thresholds and minimal attribution in flat regions
Well-presented paper: clear motivation, effective problem formulation, good visualizations, and logical flow
weaknesses: Core experimental setup undermines central claims: The paper claims to learn from unknown constraints, but uses script-generated labels based on perfect knowledge of the true cost function and budget. This is inconsistent with the problem formulation. The method should be tested with label noise, inconsistent annotations, or truly unknown label generation processes to validate claims about robustness

Weak theoretical justification for Assumption 3.6: The monotonicity requirement (safety probability can only decrease) is justified by analogy to cumulative non-negative costs in CMDPs, but the paper learns from binary labels, not costs. The relationship is more complex and deserves deeper analysis of when this assumption holds or fails

Unquantified approximation error: The use of Jensen's inequality to derive the tractable constraint (Eq. 9-10) introduces a gap whose tightness is not analyzed. Performance gaps on some tasks (Walker2d: 24.1 vs. oracle 10.3) suggest this approximation can be loose

Significant dependence on pre-training without proper ablation: The method requires pre-training on the DSRL offline dataset to 95% accuracy before online RL. The amount of data, sensitivity to initialization, and impact of this phase are not characterized. Missing ablation starting from scratch

Inconsistent architectural descriptions: The decoder output is described as log P̂ᐃ_t in the main text but as negative lognormal distribution parameters in Appendix C.2, creating confusion about the actual architecture and whether sampling introduces variance

Selective feedback mechanism lacks clear justification: Table 3 shows selective feedback (using CV method) vs. using all trajectories produces comparable results, undermining the complexity added by the coefficient-of-variation selection mechanism

Limited analysis of failure modes: On PointCircle1 (cost 16.2 vs. RLSF 1.6) and HalfCheetah (cost 22.4 vs. RLSF 0.5), SSV significantly underperforms without discussion of diagnostic tools or corrective measures

Restricted experimental scope: All tasks use synthetic binary costs and fixed budgets with script-based labels, not real human feedback. Scalability to high-dimensional states, multi-agent settings, or realistic constraints remains unclear
Unfair baseline comparison: RLSF is evaluated with the same binary label script as TraCeS, making it difficult to assess the true benefit of learning both cost and budget vs. just cost
Missing reproducibility details: Decoder module architecture incompletely specified, pre-training procedure not fully detailed, and computational overhead not analyzed

strengths: Novel problem formulation: Learning per-step violation credit from sparse trajectory-level labels is well-motivated and addresses a practical gap between dense cost supervision and available trajectory labels

Elegant technical approach: The factorization of non-violation probability into multiplicative per-step credits (Proposition 4.2) provides an interpretable framework for credit assignment without knowing cost/threshold

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 12 tasks across 3 benchmark suites with extensive ablations (low-data regimes, label noise, checkpoint sparsity, hyperparameter sensitivity) demonstrating robustness
Strong empirical label efficiency: Achieves constraint satisfaction with ~50% fewer labeled trajectories than zero-knowledge baseline and remains competitive with partial-knowledge method (RLSF)

Principled mathematical framework: Uses appropriate probabilistic modeling (binary cross-entropy loss), sound assumptions (monotone violations), and proper Jensen inequality reformulation for policy optimization
Excellent reproducibility: Detailed hyperparameters, implementation details, pseudo-code, and promise of code release
weaknesses: Loose theoretical guarantees: Jensen-gap bound (Theorem 4.5) becomes vacuous for practical horizons (e.g., ε ≈ exp(-7000) for T=1000), creating a substantial theory-practice gap that is acknowledged but not resolved

Limited experimental scope: Only simulation environments with oracle costs used for label construction; no real-world validation. Narrow domain focus (only continuous control); weak human feedback study (100 trajectories, 1 task, 3 seeds)

Comparison fairness concerns: RLSF comparison confounded by different trajectory selection strategies (novelty vs CV). Zero-knowledge C-T baseline is quite weak (ill-posed joint cost-threshold learning). Label efficiency claims primarily vs weak baselines

Strong assumptions with limited validation: Monotone violation assumption (Assumption 3.1) doesn't handle reversible safety constraints; assumes consistent, stationary labeling rule Ψ without mechanisms for drift; unclear robustness to violated assumptions

Design choices appear ad-hoc: Log-credit clamping at -7 is heuristic without principled justification; network architecture (2-stack GRU dim-4, [64,64] MLPs) lacks ablation studies; negative log-normal choice not justified vs alternatives

Dependency on offline pretraining: Table 9 shows random initialization works but with degraded performance, limiting true cold-start applicability and suggesting the method relies on good initialization

strengths: Well-motivated problem: learning safety from sparse trajectory-level labels addresses a genuine practical gap in cases where dense per-step costs are unavailable

Comprehensive experimental scope with 12 tasks across multiple benchmark suites and extensive ablations covering low-data regimes, label noise robustness, human feedback, and architectural sensitivity
Clear technical presentation of the factorization, architecture, and pipeline with sensible design choices like negative lognormal distributions to enforce probability constraints
Practical contributions including CV-based trajectory selection for reducing annotation burden and support for both terminal and checkpoint-level labels
Honest limitations discussion acknowledging constraint violations during training, labeling pipeline requirements, and consistency assumptions
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the factorization (Prop 4.2) follows straightforwardly from the chain rule; the architecture is standard (GRU + MLP); no comparison to whether the factorization structure actually helps versus learning trajectory acceptability directly

Weak theoretical contribution: the Jensen gap bound (Theorem 4.5) is acknowledged as a 'worst-case diagnostic bound' that is too loose for long horizons (ε ~ exp(-7T) for T=1000 steps), providing no actionable insight into approximation quality

Core monotonicity assumption (Assumption 3.1) is critical but under-validated: not all real safety violations are monotone; no empirical validation of when this holds; no analysis of failure modes when violated; minimal human study that doesn't test monotonicity

Problematic experimental protocol: labels constructed from oracle costs assumes the cumulative-cost model correctly captures safety; doesn't validate whether learned credits generalize to truly implicit constraints with different underlying structure

Weak zero-knowledge baseline: C-T baseline acknowledged as 'tricky' and showing 'erratic performance'; no comparison to direct binary classification, structured label propagation, or proper uncertainty sampling methods; RLSF's threshold knowledge advantage underdiscussed

Insufficient analysis of learned credits: Figures 4-6 show qualitative agreement but lack quantitative evaluation (e.g., correlation with oracle costs); no ablation demonstrating that factorization helps over direct learning of trajectory acceptability

Limited real-world validation: human study is small-scale (100 labels, 3 seeds, 1 task, only 'falling' violation); all simulation-based with no robotics, autonomous driving, or safety-critical deployment; label consistency assumption not validated on real data

Under-justified design choices: GRU hidden dim=4 seems arbitrarily small; decoder [64,64] lacks sensitivity analysis; checkpoint intervals differ by task (5 vs 20 steps); CV-based selection is heuristic without clear justification versus proper epistemic uncertainty measures

Scalability concerns: all tasks involve continuous control with 100-1000 step horizons; unclear how method scales to longer horizons, discrete actions, or image-based domains; long-horizon evaluation relies on clamping trick (log P̂ᵗ ≥ -7) that is under-analyzed

Important ablations missing: no factorization ablation comparing to direct P̂(ψ=1|τ) learning; no architecture sensitivity study; insufficient analysis of how learned credit quality affects final policy; limited justification for d and checkpoint interval selection

strengths: Well-motivated problem with practical relevance: sparse trajectory-level labels are realistic supervision when dense per-step costs are unavailable; autonomous driving example effectively illustrates context-dependent safety

Elegant theoretical framework: multiplicative factorization of non-violation probability (Prop 4.2) is interpretable; Jensen gap bound (Thm 4.5) provides principled approximation analysis; clear connection between surrogate and true constraints

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 12 tasks with extensive ablations covering label noise (C.11), trajectory selection (C.8), hyperparameter sensitivity (d, clamping, sparsity), and human feedback, demonstrating label efficiency gains over zero-knowledge baseline
Strong qualitative analysis showing learned credits localize near violations (Figs 3-6, 16-18) and trajectory-level acceptability scores are well-calibrated despite sparse binary training signal
Excellent reproducibility: code availability promised, detailed hyperparameters (Table 2), comprehensive implementation details (Appendix B.3), 8 random seeds, clear algorithm pseudo-code
Clear presentation with good visual aids and honest limitations discussion (Appendix E) addressing training-time constraint violations, labeling burden, and consistency assumptions
weaknesses: Jensen's inequality bound becomes extremely loose for long horizons: with clamp at log P̂_t ≥ -7 and T=1000, ε ≈ exp(-7000); while variance reduction argument (Remark 4.6) is intuitive, empirical analysis of bound tightness on evaluated tasks is missing

Limited real-world validation: all experiments use oracle costs to generate labels (ensuring perfect consistency unlike real human labels); human feedback study is small scale (100 trajectories, 3 seeds, 1 task) with overlapping confidence intervals; no deployed system evaluation

Realizability assumptions in Lemma 4.4 are stated informally ('if p̂_τ is a good proxy'); sufficient estimator capacity and small optimization error are required but not formalized; guidance on diagnosing when assumptions fail is limited

Restrictive monotone violation assumption (Assumption 3.1) excludes realistic scenarios where violations can be recovered from; while acknowledged in limitations, this significantly constrains applicability without empirical study of non-monotone settings

Incomplete baseline comparisons: C-T baseline is newly designed rather than established zero-knowledge method; RLSF has partial knowledge (known threshold) making comparison not entirely fair; Table 6 (matched budgets) shows TraCeS competitive but not uniformly better than RLSF; missing comparisons to reward thresholding or other constraint learning methods

Technical details underspecified: why GRU with hidden dimension 4? coefficient of variation for trajectory selection justified informally; distribution shift from behavior to policy only addressed through iterative retraining without formal analysis; guidance on choosing d in practice is limited despite C.10 sensitivity study
